import FormalConjecturesUtil

/-!
# Erdős Problem 457

*Reference:* [erdosproblems.com/457](https://www.erdosproblems.com/457)
-/

namespace Erdos457

/--
Is there some $\epsilon > 0$ such that there are infinitely
many $n$ where all primes $p \le (2 + \epsilon) \log n$ divide
$$
  \prod_{1 \le i \le \log n} (n + i)?
$$

This was formalized in Lean by Baretto and van Doorn using Aristotle.
-/
@[category research solved, AMS 11, formal_proof using lean4 at "https://github.com/Woett/Lean-files/blob/main/ErdosProblem457.lean"]
theorem erdos_457 : answer(True) ↔ ∃ ε > (0 : ℝ),
    { (n : ℕ) | ∀ (p : ℕ), p ≤ (2 + ε) * Real.log n → p.Prime →
      p ∣ ∏ i ∈ Finset.Icc 1 ⌊Real.log n⌋₊, (n + i) }.Infinite := by
  sorry

/-- Let $q(n, k)$ denote the least prime which does not divide
$\prod_{1 \le i \le k}(n + i)$. -/
noncomputable abbrev q (n : ℕ) (k : ℝ) : ℕ :=
    Nat.find (Nat.exists_prime_not_dvd (n := ∏ i ∈ Finset.Icc 1 ⌊k⌋₊, (n + i))
      (Finset.prod_ne_zero_iff.2 fun a ha => by aesop))

/--
More generally, let $q(n, k)$ denote the least prime which
does not divide $\prod_{1 \le i \le k}(n + i)$. This
problem asks whether $q(n, \log n) \ge (2 + \epsilon) \log n$
infinitely often.
-/
@[category research open, AMS 11]
theorem erdos_457.variants.qnk : answer(sorry) ↔ ∃ ε > (0 : ℝ),
    { (n : ℕ) | (2 + ε) * Real.log n ≤ q n (Real.log n) }.Infinite := by
  sorry

/--
Taking $n$ to be the product of primes
between $\log n$ and $(2 + o(1)) \log n$ gives an example where
$$
  q(n, \log n) \ge (2 + o(1)) \log n.
$$
Can one prove that $q(n, \log n) < (1 - \epsilon) (\log n)^2$
for all large $n$ and some $\epsilon > 0$?
-/
@[category research open, AMS 11]
theorem erdos_457.variants.one_sub : answer(sorry) ↔ ∃ ε > (0 : ℝ),
    ∀ᶠ n in Filter.atTop, q n (Real.log n) < (1 - ε) * Real.log n ^ 2 := by
  sorry

end Erdos457

status_issues.source_status: Solved affirmatively, with a Lean-verified proof. The updated source credits GPT-5.2 Pro, prompted by Kevin Barreto, with a construction improving the constant 2 to 3/log 4, and records subsequent stronger bounds. This variant is equivalent to the main question, which the file already marks solved.
status_issues.evidence: The 2026-08-24 snapshot of https://www.erdosproblems.com/457, last edited 7 March 2026, says “PROVED (LEAN)” and explicitly identifies q(n,log n) ≥ (2 + ε) log n infinitely often as the same problem. The current teorth database also records problem 457 as “proved (Lean)”. The cited external proof establishes the divisibility statement with ε = 0.1.
status_issues.suggested_change: Change the category to research solved and replace answer(sorry) with answer(True). The cited proof of the main theorem also implies this variant.

reformulations.difference: The variant uses q(n, log n) ≥ (2 + ε) log n, whereas divisibility by every prime p ≤ (2 + ε) log n corresponds pointwise to the strict inequality q(n, log n) > (2 + ε) log n. The source itself presents the non-strict version as a reformulation.
reformulations.equivalence_argument: For any real bound B, every prime p ≤ B divides the product iff B < q(n,k), by the defining minimality and nondivisibility of q. Thus the divisibility question implies the non-strict q question with the same ε. Conversely, given the non-strict q bound for infinitely many n with some ε > 0, discard n ≤ 1 and replace ε by ε/2. Positivity of log n then gives (2 + ε/2) log n < (2 + ε) log n ≤ q(n,log n), yielding the divisibility statement. The full equivalence of the existential infinitude statements was proved in the scratch file without sorry or reliance on the problem theorems.

review.notes: Checked all four declarations. The definition q has the intended least-prime semantics; the product is always nonzero, and natural flooring selects exactly the integer indices 1 ≤ i ≤ k. Lean checks covered empty products, q(n,k) = 2 for k < 1, the n = 0 and n = 1 logarithmic cases, and small integer examples. The upper-bound variant one_sub faithfully matches the still-open problem now listed as #1181. Scratch proofs are in /workspace/review/scratch.lean. The cited external proof has the same mathematical statement; after compatibility-only edits in a sandbox copy, it kernel-checks with only propext, Classical.choice, and Quot.sound. Live erdosproblems.com requests were Cloudflare-blocked, so source verification used archived pages and the current status database.
